notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg2200.tlg00401.opp-gr: 245: 'two boys' and 'the two corpses' are duals. 247: it is unclear whether Libanius or his visitors say 'I will be gone by tomorrow'; taken as his own words. 248: the relative clause may instead mean that the friends believed these people to be the craftsmen. 249: 'my classroom' renders 'the chorus of speeches', Libanius's term for his school. 250: the text is broken at 'τύχης τοίνυν ρας'; something is lost before 'ρας', and the last sentence is translated from what can be read.

nodes.text: While I was in this state, I had a dream of this sort. I dreamt that some people had sacrificed two boys and placed one of the two corpses in a temple of Zeus, behind the door; and when I was indignant at the outrage to Zeus, some said that it would stay like this until evening, and that when evening came it would be given burial. This seemed to signify drugs and spells and a war waged by sorcerers.

And the event followed: those fears, and a longing for nothing but death. Instead, there was talk of this to whoever was with me at the time, and prayers for it to the gods. Hateful was anyone who mentioned a bath, hateful anyone who mentioned dinner; there was flight from the books in which the labours of the ancients lie, flight from writing and composing speeches; speaking had been given up, and that while the young men demanded it with shouts. For whenever I did set about it, I was carried back, like a skiff by a contrary wind, and while they had hopes of a hearing, I for my part fell silent. The doctors told me to seek the cure for these things elsewhere, since there were no such drugs in their art.

This too seemed to them and to the others to come from the same source: that my joints became diseased twice, which had never happened before, in winter and in summer, and that it gave those who came to see me cause always to say that I would be gone by the next day. In the other cities I was even thought to have died, and they kept asking the many embassies whether this was so.

There were some of my friends who were stirring both me and themselves up against certain people who were reputed to be the craftsmen of these things; but I was not myself moved in any such way, and I held them back, saying that we ought to pray rather than drag people [to court] over things put together in darkness.

And yet a chameleon appeared, from where I do not know, in my classroom: this chameleon had been [dead] a long time, a corpse of not a few months; we saw its head lying between its hind feet, and of the other feet one was nowhere, while the other was closing its mouth into silence.

Even so, despite such great things laid bare, I did not bring anyone's name [before a court] over what had come to light; but fear did seem to me to come over those who were conscious of something, and they let up from their persistence, and it became possible for me to move again. It was [the work] of fortune, then, [...] that the things which had been buried lay above ground for any who wished to see.
